notes.front: What is a token, and roughly how many tokens is a page of English?
notes.back:
A token is a chunk of text (often a subword, sometimes a whole word or a single character) that the model actually reads and writes. The model never sees letters or words — only token IDs from a fixed vocabulary of ~50k–250k entries.

"unbelievable" → un believ able (3 tokens).
Rule of thumb for English: 1 token ≈ ¾ of a word ≈ 4 characters. A dense A4 page (~500 words) ≈ 650–700 tokens.

notes.front: Why do LLMs miscount the letters in “strawberry”?
notes.back:
Because the model never sees individual letters. "strawberry" arrives as one or two tokens (e.g. str awberry). Asking "how many r's" requires the model to have memorised the spelling of the token, which it only partially has. Same root cause for weak anagrams, reversing strings, and rhyming.

Ask a model to spell "strawberry" letter by letter first — it usually then counts correctly, because now each letter is its own token.

notes.front: How does Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) build a vocabulary?
notes.back:
Start with single characters/bytes. Repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair in the training corpus and merge it into a new token. Stop when the vocabulary reaches the target size. Frequent strings become single tokens; rare ones stay fragmented.

Corpus full of "the" → merges t+h→th, then th+e→the. A rare surname stays as 4–5 fragments.

Consequence: the tokenizer is frozen at training time; it encodes what was common in that corpus.

notes.front: Why does the same sentence cost more tokens in Dutch (or Thai, or JSON) than in English?
notes.back:
The tokenizer was trained mostly on English, so English words get single tokens while other languages fragment into smaller pieces. More tokens = higher cost, slower generation, and less effective context.

"gemeentelijke belastingaanslag" might be 8–10 tokens; the English "municipal tax assessment" ~4. Dutch text typically runs 1.3–2× the English token count. Thai/Hindi can run 3–5×. JSON with lots of quotes, braces and whitespace also inflates.
"Supports 100 languages" — ask: at what token efficiency and at what benchmark quality per language? Support ≠ parity.

notes.front: Why do models sometimes claim 9.11 > 9.9?
notes.back:
Numbers are tokenized arbitrarily (9 . 11 vs 9 . 9), so the model has no built-in numeric representation — it pattern-matches on token sequences. "9.11" also looks like a date, a version number, or a bible verse, all of which "come after" 9.9.

Newer tokenizers split digits individually or in groups of three to reduce this, but arithmetic remains learned behaviour, not computation. For real math, give the model a calculator/code tool.

notes.front: What problem does attention solve? Give the classic example.
notes.back:
For each position, it lets the model ask "which other tokens in the input matter for interpreting this one?" and pull information from them, weighted by relevance. It replaces the fixed-window or sequential bottleneck of older models.

"The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." — it attends strongly to animal.
"…because it was too wide." — it now attends to street. Same word, different attention pattern, decided by the surrounding context.

notes.front: Explain Query, Key, Value (Q/K/V) with an intuitive analogy.
notes.back:
Each token produces three vectors:

Query = what I am looking for. Key = what I advertise about myself. Value = what I hand over if selected.

A token's query is compared (dot product) against every other token's key → similarity scores → softmax → weights. Output = weighted sum of the values.

Library: you walk in with a question (query), scan the labels on the spines (keys), and take the contents of the best-matching books (values), blended in proportion to how well each label matched.

notes.front: What is multi-head attention and why have more than one head?
notes.back:
Run several independent attention computations in parallel, each with its own Q/K/V projections, then concatenate. Each head can learn a different relationship.

In one layer, head 3 might link pronouns to their referents, head 7 might link a closing bracket to its opening bracket, head 12 might attend to the previous token. Interpretability work has found such specialised heads in real models.

notes.front: Why is attention O(n²) in the sequence length, and what does that mean in practice?
notes.back:
Every token computes a score against every other token: n tokens → n×n scores. Doubling the input quadruples the attention compute and the memory for those scores.

8k → 128k context is 16× the length but 256× the attention work. This is why long-context calls cost more, why "1M context" needs tricks (sparse/linear attention, sliding windows, FlashAttention for memory), and why prefill of a huge prompt takes seconds before the first output token appears.

notes.front: What are the two main sub-blocks in a transformer layer, and what does each do?
notes.back:
1. Attention — moves information between positions ("look at other tokens").
2. Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) / feed-forward block — processes each position independently ("think about what I've gathered"). Most of the parameters live here; it is where much factual recall appears to be stored.

A model stacks dozens of these layers (e.g. 32–120). Each layer refines the representation of every token; by the last layer, the final token's representation is used to predict the next token.

notes.front: What does “autoregressive” mean, and why does it matter for cost and latency?
notes.back:
The model produces one token at a time; each new token is appended to the input and the model runs again. There is no plan or draft — only the next token, repeatedly.

A 500-token answer = 500 forward passes. Output tokens are therefore far more expensive than input tokens (typically 3–5× the price) and generation speed is measured in tokens/second (~30–150 t/s is typical for hosted models).

This is also why "let the model think step by step" works: generating intermediate tokens gives it more compute per problem.

notes.front: What is the KV cache and what explains “first token slow, rest fast”?
notes.back:
During generation, the keys and values for all previous tokens are stored so they are not recomputed for every new token. That is the Key-Value (KV) cache.

Prefill: the whole prompt is processed at once — compute-heavy, gives you the time-to-first-token. Decode: each subsequent token only attends to the cache — cheap per token, but memory-bound.

A 100k-token prompt on a 70B model can need tens of GB of KV cache per request. This is why long-context serving is expensive and why providers offer "prompt caching" discounts for reusing the same prefix.

notes.front: Attention is order-blind. How does the model know word order?
notes.back:
Plain attention treats the input as a set — "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical. Positional encodings inject position information, either added to embeddings (original transformer) or by rotating Q/K vectors by position (Rotary Position Embedding, RoPE, the current standard).

Because positions are learned within a range, a model trained at 8k tokens does not automatically work at 128k; extending context requires retraining or interpolation tricks (e.g. YaRN). "Extended to 1M context" often means such a trick was applied post hoc, with quality degrading at the far end.

notes.front: What does temperature do? Is temperature 0 “deterministic reasoning”?
notes.back:
The model outputs a probability for every vocabulary token. Temperature rescales those probabilities before sampling: low = sharpen (pick the top choice almost always), high = flatten (more random). Temperature 0 = greedy: always the single most likely token.

Prompt "The capital of France is" → 98% "Paris", 1% "a", … At T=0 you get Paris every time; at T=1.5 you sometimes get "a city…".
T=0 is not "more correct" or "reasoning mode" — it just removes sampling noise. It can lock in a wrong first token. And hosted models at T=0 are still not bit-for-bit reproducible (batching, floating-point nondeterminism).

notes.front: What exactly is inside the context window on a single API call?
notes.back:
Everything the model can see, in one flat token sequence: system prompt + tool definitions + all prior user/assistant messages + any documents you pasted or retrieved + the tokens it has generated so far. The window is the hard cap on that total.

A 128k model with a 3k system prompt, 40 tool definitions (~8k), and a 100k PDF leaves ~17k for conversation and answer. When you exceed it, the call fails or the oldest messages are silently dropped by the client.

notes.front: Does a chatbot “remember” the conversation? What actually happens each turn?
notes.back:
No. The model is stateless. Every turn, the client re-sends the entire transcript (plus the new message) and the model reads it all from scratch. "Memory" features are just software that stores notes and re-injects them into the prompt.

Turn 1 costs 500 tokens. Turn 20 of the same chat costs the full 20-turn transcript (~15k tokens) — every time. Long chats get slower and more expensive per message, and old details can fall out of the window.

notes.front: What is the “lost in the middle” effect?
notes.back:
Models retrieve facts placed at the start or end of a long context more reliably than facts buried in the middle. Accuracy can drop noticeably for mid-context information, especially in older or smaller models.

Put the key clause of a contract at position 60k of a 120k-token prompt and ask about it; put the same clause at position 2k; compare. Practical fix: put the most important material first or last, and summarise/rank rather than dumping.

notes.front: What does a “needle in a haystack” test measure, and what does it not?
notes.back:
A single unrelated fact ("the secret code is 4711") is hidden somewhere in a long filler text and the model is asked to retrieve it. Passing shows the model can address any position in the window.

It does not show the model can reason over the whole window: combine many scattered facts, notice contradictions, or summarise faithfully. Those degrade much earlier than needle retrieval.

"99% needle accuracy at 1M tokens" is the weakest possible long-context claim. Ask for multi-needle, aggregation, or real-task results at that length.

notes.front: Marketing check: “1M token context window.” What questions expose whether it is useful?
notes.back:
1. What is the effective context — at what length does task accuracy start dropping?
2. What does a single 1M-token call cost and how long is time-to-first-token?
3. Is that length native (trained at it) or extended post hoc?
4. Do output limits scale too, or is it 1M in / 8k out?
5. Does it hold on my content (code, tables, Dutch) or on English prose benchmarks?

Rule of thumb: assume quality is solid at ⅓–½ of the advertised window and verify beyond that.

notes.front: If a model has a 200k context, why not just paste all the documents instead of building RAG?
notes.back:
Sometimes you should — "long-context stuffing" beats a bad RAG pipeline for small corpora. Reasons to still retrieve:

Cost: 150k tokens per question adds up fast. Latency: seconds of prefill. Precision: irrelevant text dilutes attention and raises hallucination. Scale: 10,000 documents don't fit no matter what. Freshness: retrieval reads the current version at query time.

One 40-page policy handbook → stuff it in (maybe with prompt caching). A 50 GB SharePoint → retrieve.

notes.front: What is pretraining, and why is a base model not a chatbot?
notes.back:
Pretraining = predicting the next token over trillions of tokens of internet text, code, and books. The result is a base model: a very good autocomplete, with no notion of "answering" or "being helpful".

Prompt a base model with "What is the capital of France?" and it may continue "What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Spain?" — because that is what such text often looks like on the web (a quiz page).

Nearly all capability comes from pretraining; later stages mostly shape behaviour.

notes.front: What do Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) add on top of a base model?
notes.back:
SFT: train on curated (prompt → ideal answer) pairs so the model learns the assistant format: answer the question, stop, use the chat template.

RLHF (and variants like Direct Preference Optimization, DPO): show humans pairs of answers, learn which they prefer, optimise the model toward preferred answers. This is where helpfulness, tone, refusals — and also sycophancy and verbosity — come from.

The same base model after different post-training becomes a terse coding assistant or a chatty companion. "Aligned" is a training artefact, not a property of the weights' knowledge.

notes.front: What is fine-tuning genuinely good for? Give three examples.
notes.back:
Changing how the model behaves — form, style, and reliability on a narrow, repeated task:

1. Always emitting your exact JSON schema without a 2k-token instruction.
2. Adopting a house writing style or a specific tone consistently.
3. Classifying support tickets into your 40 categories with a small, cheap model instead of a large one.

Typical dataset: hundreds to low thousands of high-quality examples. Payoff: shorter prompts, lower latency, cheaper model doing the job of a bigger one.

notes.front: Why is “fine-tune the model on our documentation so it knows our product” usually the wrong plan?
notes.back:
Fine-tuning changes behaviour far more efficiently than it adds facts. Knowledge injected this way is fuzzy, hard to update, and the model still hallucinates confidently around the edges of what it absorbed.

Fine-tune on your API docs → the model learns your naming style and produces plausible-looking endpoints, including ones that don't exist. Change a parameter next month → retrain, re-evaluate, redeploy. With RAG you just replace the document.
"Trained on your data" — ask: fine-tuned or retrieved? How do updates propagate? Is my data isolated from other tenants' weights?

notes.front: What is Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) / Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)?
notes.back:
Instead of updating all weights (billions of parameters, huge GPU memory), freeze the base model and train small low-rank adapter matrices inserted into each layer. Typically under 1% of the parameters; adapters are a few hundred MB and can be swapped per customer.

One 70B base model, 50 customers each with their own 200 MB LoRA adapter, served from the same GPUs. This is how "custom model per tenant" is usually implemented.

Same limitations as full fine-tuning: great for behaviour, poor for injecting facts.

notes.front: What is distillation?
notes.back:
Training a smaller "student" model on the outputs (or output distributions) of a larger "teacher" model, so the small model imitates the large one on a target domain.

Generate 100k labelled examples with a frontier model, fine-tune an 8B open model on them, deploy the 8B at 1/20 the cost. Works well for narrow tasks; the student will not match the teacher on out-of-distribution inputs.

Much of the "small model beats a big one" news is distillation on the benchmark's domain.

notes.front: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in one sentence, with an example?
notes.back:
At question time, find the most relevant pieces of your own documents and paste them into the prompt so the model answers from that text instead of from its training memory.

Employee asks "how many days of parental leave do I get?" → system searches the HR handbook, finds the leave section, builds the prompt: [leave policy text] … Using only the text above, answer: how many days…

The model does not "learn" anything; it just reads what you hand it, every single call.

notes.front: What are the steps of a standard RAG pipeline, and where does it usually break?
notes.back:
Offline: split documents into chunks → compute an embedding vector per chunk → store in a vector index.
Online: embed the user question → find the top-k most similar chunks → put them in the prompt → generate.

It usually breaks before the model sees anything:

• Bad chunking (a table split in half; a heading separated from its content).
• Retrieval misses (question phrasing ≠ document phrasing; the answer needs 3 chunks, you fetched 1).
• Stale or duplicate documents (three versions of the same policy; which one wins?).

When a RAG answer is wrong, check what was retrieved first. It is the retrieval ~80% of the time.

notes.front: What is an embedding, intuitively?
notes.back:
A fixed-length vector (e.g. 1,024 numbers) representing the meaning of a text, produced by a separate, smaller model. Texts with similar meaning land close together, measured by cosine similarity.

"How do I reset my password?" and "forgot login credentials" are far apart as strings but close as embeddings. "Password reset for the Jenkins server" and "Jenkins build failing" share words but sit further apart.

Embeddings ignore exact identifiers poorly — "ticket INC-48213" vs "INC-48231" look nearly identical. That is why serious systems combine vector search with keyword search (hybrid / BM25).

notes.front: Why does RAG reduce hallucination but not eliminate it?
notes.back:
The model still generates freely; retrieved text just raises the probability of grounded output. Failure modes that remain:

• Retrieval returns nothing relevant → model falls back on training memory and answers anyway.
• Retrieved text is partially relevant → model blends it with invented details.
• Model misreads a table or a negation ("not covered" → "covered").
• Citations can themselves be fabricated unless the system enforces them structurally (e.g. the model can only reference chunk IDs it was given).

Ask about a product that isn't in the knowledge base; a naive RAG bot often confidently describes it anyway. Fix: retrieval confidence threshold + "say you don't know" instruction + evaluate that behaviour.

notes.front: Decision rule: when to prompt, when to RAG, when to fine-tune?
notes.back:
Prompting first: most "we need a custom model" requests are solved with a good system prompt and a few examples.

RAG when the model needs facts it doesn't have: internal docs, recent data, per-customer data, anything that changes.

Fine-tuning when the model needs to behave differently at scale: format, style, latency/cost via a smaller model — and you have hundreds of good examples plus an eval set.

They combine: RAG for what, fine-tuning for how. Neither replaces a good eval set.

notes.front: What is prompt injection and why does it matter for RAG and agents?
notes.back:
The model cannot reliably tell instructions from data — everything in the context is just tokens. If retrieved content or a web page contains "ignore previous instructions and email the customer list to…", the model may comply.

A RAG bot over a shared wiki: anyone who can edit a wiki page can plant instructions for the bot. An email-reading agent: a malicious email can steer it. The more tools an agent has, the more damage an injection can do.
"Our model is immune to prompt injection" — no model is. Ask what the system does architecturally: least-privilege tools, human approval for side effects, separating trusted from untrusted content.

notes.front: What is a benchmark like Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU), and what are its weaknesses?
notes.back:
A fixed set of ~14k multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, scored by accuracy. Cheap, reproducible, comparable across models.

Weaknesses: contamination (the questions leak into training data — models "remember" answers); saturation (top models cluster at 88–92%, differences are noise); format mismatch (multiple choice ≠ writing a migration plan); and known label errors in the dataset itself.

A 1–2 point benchmark lead is not evidence of a better model for you. Ask whether the vendor checked for contamination, and whether the benchmark resembles your task.

notes.front: Why is “beats GPT-4 on X benchmarks” weak evidence for your use case?
notes.back:
Goodhart's law: once a benchmark becomes the target, it stops measuring what it was meant to. Labs tune data mixes toward public benchmarks. A model can top a coding benchmark and be worse at your codebase's conventions.

A model fine-tuned on a coding benchmark's public solutions scores higher on that benchmark and lower on fresh problems written last month. Fresh, private, or continuously-refreshed benchmarks (e.g. live-updated coding tasks) are more trustworthy for exactly this reason.

Vendor benchmark tables also cherry-pick: which benchmarks, which prompting setup, how many attempts.

notes.front: What does pass@k mean, and how can it inflate a coding score?
notes.back:
pass@k = the probability that at least one of k generated attempts passes the tests. pass@1 is "first try works"; pass@10 lets the model try ten times.

A model with 40% pass@1 may show 75% pass@10. A headline "solves 75% of problems" that is secretly pass@10, with majority voting, and with extra tool use, describes a very different product than what a user gets on a single call.
Always ask: how many attempts, with what tools, and was the score verified by a third party?

notes.front: What is “LLM-as-a-judge” and what biases does it have?
notes.back:
Using a strong model to grade another model's outputs (score 1–10, or pick the better of two). Cheap and scalable compared with human review, and correlates reasonably with human preference on many tasks.

Known biases: length (longer looks better), position (the first of two answers wins more often), self-preference (a model rates its own family higher), style over substance (confident, well-formatted wrong answers score well).

Mitigations: swap answer order and average; give the judge a rubric and a reference answer; spot-check 5–10% of judgements with humans.

notes.front: What do human-preference arenas (Elo leaderboards) measure, and what don't they?
notes.back:
Users type a prompt, get two anonymous answers, vote for the better one; votes produce an Elo-style ranking. It measures "which answer do people prefer in a chat" on the prompts people happen to type.

It does not measure correctness (users often can't verify), long-horizon tasks, tool use, or your domain. Rankings are sensitive to style: chattier, more formatted, more confident answers gain Elo. Vendors have been shown to test many private variants and publish only the best.

Top of an arena ≈ "pleasant chat model", not "most accurate model".

notes.front: What is the minimum evaluation setup you should insist on before deploying an LLM feature?
notes.back:
A golden set: 50–300 real inputs from your actual use case, each with an expected output or a grading rubric, stored in version control, run automatically on every prompt/model/pipeline change.

Support-bot: 150 real tickets + the approved answers. Score: correct/partially/wrong, plus "did it say I-don't-know when it should". Track the number per release like a test suite. When the vendor releases model v2, run the set before switching — "better on benchmarks" regularly means worse on a specific task.

Without this you cannot distinguish "the new model is better" from "the demo happened to work".

notes.front: How do you evaluate a RAG system in two separate layers?
notes.back:
Retrieval layer: for each test question, did the right chunk(s) appear in the top-k? Metrics: recall@k, precision@k, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). No LLM needed.

Generation layer: given the retrieved chunks, is the answer faithful (only claims supported by the chunks), relevant (answers the question), and complete?

If recall@5 is 60%, no prompt engineering will fix the 40% of questions where the answer was never in the prompt. Fix chunking/embeddings/hybrid search first, then tune the prompt.

notes.front: Marketing check: “99% accuracy.” What are the five follow-up questions?
notes.back:
1. Accuracy on what task and what dataset — theirs or a public one?
2. Who measured it — the vendor, or a third party?
3. N — how many examples? 99% of 100 is 1 error; the confidence interval is wide.
4. What counts as correct — exact match, human judgement, LLM judge?
5. Under what conditions — single attempt, no tools, same latency and cost as the product I'd buy?

A number without these is a slogan.

notes.front: What does “70B parameters” mean, and why is parameter count a weak proxy for quality?
notes.back:
70 billion learned weights (numbers). In 16-bit precision that is ~140 GB of memory just to load — hence GPU requirements. Parameter count sets a capacity ceiling, but data quality, training tokens, and post-training decide what you get.

A well-trained 8B model from this year routinely beats a 70B model from three years ago. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models muddy it further: "400B total parameters" may only use ~20B active per token — compute cost like a 20B model, memory like a 400B model.
"Our 1-trillion-parameter model" tells you about hosting cost, not capability.

notes.front: What is quantization and what is the trade-off?
notes.back:
Storing weights in fewer bits (16-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit) to cut memory and speed up inference. A 70B model at 4-bit fits in ~40 GB instead of ~140 GB.

8-bit: usually negligible quality loss. 4-bit: small but measurable degradation, worse on math/code and long reasoning. Below 4-bit: noticeable. A cheap API "running Model X" may be serving a heavily quantized version — same name, lower quality.
Ask hosting providers what precision they serve at.

notes.front: What is a “reasoning” or “thinking” model, mechanically?
notes.back:
A model post-trained (via reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks like math and code) to generate a long chain of intermediate tokens before its final answer. Same transformer, same next-token prediction — just spending more tokens (compute) per question. "Test-time compute scaling."

A hard math question: standard model answers in 200 tokens and is wrong; the reasoning model generates 8,000 tokens of working, catches an error mid-way, and is right. You pay for all 8,000 tokens and wait 30 seconds.
Reasoning modes help on multi-step, verifiable problems and can be worse — or just slower and pricier — on simple extraction, chat, or writing.

notes.front: What is an “agent”, and why do agent demos look better than agent products?
notes.back:
An LLM in a loop: model outputs a structured tool call (e.g. search_tickets(status="open")) → software executes it → result goes back into the context → model decides the next step → repeat until done. The model never runs anything; the harness does.

If each step is 95% reliable, a 10-step task succeeds ~60% of the time (0.9510), and a 30-step task ~21%. Demos show the happy path once; products face the compounding.
Ask: success rate over N runs on real tasks, how failures are detected, what needs human approval, and what the cost per completed task is.

notes.front: Why do models hallucinate, and why can't they “just say I don't know”?
notes.back:
The model is trained to produce the most plausible continuation, and post-trained to be helpful. Nothing in it checks claims against a fact store; a fluent wrong answer and a fluent right answer are produced by the same mechanism. Uncertainty is not directly represented as "I don't know" — it shows up as a flatter probability distribution, which sampling then hides.

Ask for a citation on an obscure topic → the model produces a real-looking author, journal, year, and DOI that don't exist, because that pattern is what citations look like.

Mitigations are external: grounding via RAG, tools that verify, structural constraints (only cite given IDs), and evals that punish confident wrong answers.

notes.front: Quick translation table: what do common vendor phrases usually mean in practice?
notes.back:
"Trained on your data" → usually RAG over your documents, occasionally a LoRA adapter.
"Learns from every interaction" → logs stored and re-injected into prompts; the weights don't change.
"Understands your business" → a system prompt plus retrieval.
"Enterprise-grade accuracy" → no number given; ask for the eval set.
"Proprietary model" → often an open-weights model with a fine-tune, or a wrapped frontier API.
"Agentic" → an LLM loop with tools; ask for the success rate.
"Hallucination-free" → not a thing; ask what is verified and how.
